marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q019.takeaway: The embryonic heart begins beating in the 4th week, shortly after the paired endocardial tubes fuse into the primitive heart tube.
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q019.displayText: The heart begins to beat during the 4th week of development. Cardiac development starts earlier, with cardiogenic mesoderm and paired endocardial tubes forming before the primitive heart tube becomes functional. By about day 22–23, rhythmic contractions begin, which places the onset of the heartbeat in week 4. The important exam distinction is that structural cardiac development begins before the first heartbeat; the heartbeat itself starts in the 4th week.
emphasis: heartbeat itself starts in the 4th week

rationales.a: The second week is too early; the cardiogenic field has not yet produced a functioning primitive heart tube capable of rhythmic contraction.
rationales.c: By the sixth week the embryonic heart has already been beating for several weeks, so this is too late.
rationales.d: The tenth week is far beyond the onset of cardiac activity, which begins during the fourth week.

marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q020.takeaway: Foramen ovale closes functionally at birth but anatomical fusion takes months; therefore anatomical closure by 3–5 days is the false statement.
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q020.displayText: The false statement is that the foramen ovale closes anatomically by 3–5 days. At birth, lung expansion lowers pulmonary vascular resistance and raises left atrial pressure above right atrial pressure, pressing septum primum against septum secundum and producing functional closure. Anatomical fusion is much slower: the source prose gives roughly 1 month to a year, while its table states months to years. The ductus venosus undergoes anatomical closure within about the first week, and the ductus arteriosus anatomically obliterates over roughly 2–3 weeks. The right umbilical vein normally regresses during fetal development, leaving the left umbilical vein as the persistent placental channel.
emphasis: foramen ovale closes anatomically by 3–5 days

rationales.b: Anatomical closure of the ductus venosus occurs around the first postnatal week, so 3–7 days is compatible with the source timing and is not the false statement.
rationales.c: The right umbilical vein normally regresses during development; the left umbilical vein persists to carry oxygenated placental blood, so this statement is true.
rationales.d: Anatomical closure of the ductus arteriosus occurs over about 10–21 days, commonly summarized as 2–3 weeks, so this statement is true.

marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q021.takeaway: The first visible sign of respiratory development is the laryngotracheal (respiratory) diverticulum budding from ventral foregut endoderm.
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q021.displayText: The laryngotracheal, or respiratory, diverticulum is the first sign of respiratory-system development. It appears as an outgrowth from the ventral wall of the pharyngeal foregut. Its endoderm forms the epithelial lining of the larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles and alveoli, while surrounding splanchnic mesoderm supplies respiratory-tract connective tissue, cartilage and smooth muscle. As the diverticulum elongates caudally, tracheoesophageal folds separate it from the dorsal esophagus and its distal end later branches into the bronchial buds.
emphasis: ventral wall of the pharyngeal foregut

rationales.a: The tracheoesophageal septum forms during separation of the respiratory diverticulum from the foregut, so it follows the initial appearance of the diverticulum.
rationales.b: The hypobranchial eminence contributes chiefly to tongue development and is not the first respiratory primordium.
rationales.c: The primitive foregut exists before the respiratory system begins; the specific respiratory sign is the ventral laryngotracheal diverticulum arising from it.

marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q022.takeaway: The larynx and trachea arise from the laryngotracheal tube, while its distal bronchial buds give rise to the bronchial tree and lung parenchyma.
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q022.displayText: The larynx and trachea develop from the laryngotracheal tube. The respiratory diverticulum grows from the ventral foregut and elongates caudally. Its portion cranial to the distal bifurcation forms the laryngotracheal tube and gives rise to the laryngeal and tracheal region. The caudal end divides into right and left bronchial buds, which branch repeatedly to form the bronchi and the epithelial components of the lungs. Thus the key distinction is proximal laryngotracheal tube for larynx/trachea versus distal bronchial buds for the branching lung.
emphasis: larynx and trachea develop from the laryngotracheal tube

rationales.b: The laryngotracheal groove is the early ventral foregut depression that precedes formation of the diverticulum; the formed larynx and trachea are derived from the laryngotracheal tube.
rationales.c: Lung buds are distal branches that generate the bronchial tree and lung parenchyma rather than the larynx and trachea.
rationales.d: Bronchial buds form the bronchi and downstream pulmonary branching structures, not the proximal larynx and trachea.

marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q023.takeaway: The commonest tracheoesophageal anomaly is esophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula (type C).
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q023.displayText: The most common tracheoesophageal fistula pattern is esophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula, classically called type C. The proximal esophagus ends blindly, while the distal esophageal segment communicates with the trachea. These anomalies arise from abnormal partitioning of the foregut by the tracheoesophageal septum. Clinically, esophageal atresia causes feeding difficulty and inability to pass a tube into the stomach, while a distal fistula permits air to enter the gastrointestinal tract. The discriminator is therefore proximal esophageal atresia plus distal TEF.
emphasis: esophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula
proximal esophageal atresia plus distal TEF

rationales.a: Esophageal atresia with a proximal fistula is an uncommon configuration and is not the predominant TEF pattern.
rationales.c: An isolated H-type fistula occurs without esophageal atresia and is much less common than type C.
rationales.d: A proximal fistula with distal esophageal atresia is not the usual arrangement; the common pattern has proximal atresia with a fistula involving the distal esophageal segment.

marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q024.takeaway: Lung maturation proceeds embryonic → pseudoglandular → canalicular → saccular/alveolar; the source’s missing numbered mapping prevents independent recovery of what numerals 1–4 denote.
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q024.displayText: The medically recoverable chronology is embryonic phase first, followed by pseudoglandular, canalicular and then saccular/alveolar development. In the source table, the embryonic phase spans approximately 0–7 weeks and establishes lung buds and main pulmonary arteries; the pseudoglandular phase (about 7–17 weeks) develops conducting airways toward the acinus; the canalicular phase (about 17–27 weeks) develops respiratory airways and the blood-air barrier; and the saccular/alveolar phase begins later and continues into postnatal life with alveolar development and septation. The stored question, however, presents answer choices only as numerical sequences and the rendered source does not preserve the list assigning phase names to numerals 1–4. The keyed source answer is 2-4-3-1, but that numeral-to-phase mapping cannot be reconstructed confidently from the surviving question text alone.
emphasis: pseudoglandular, canalicular and then saccular/alveolar development

rationales.a: The surviving source does not preserve which phase each numeral represents, so sequence 3-2-1-4 cannot be independently mapped to the named phases; use the recoverable named chronology rather than inventing the missing mapping.
rationales.b: The surviving source does not preserve which phase each numeral represents, so sequence 2-1-4-3 cannot be independently validated; the authoritative named chronology remains embryonic → pseudoglandular → canalicular → saccular/alveolar.
rationales.c: The surviving source does not preserve which phase each numeral represents, so sequence 4-2-1-3 cannot be independently validated; no numeral-to-phase assignment should be invented.

marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q025.takeaway: The common posterolateral congenital diaphragmatic hernia (Bochdalek) results from failure of pleuroperitoneal membrane closure and often causes ipsilateral pulmonary hypoplasia.
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q025.displayText: The infant’s bowel herniation into the left thorax with a hypoplastic left lung is characteristic of a congenital diaphragmatic hernia, most commonly a posterolateral Bochdalek defect. It results from failure of a pleuroperitoneal membrane to fuse with the other developing components of the diaphragm, leaving a posterolateral communication through which abdominal viscera enter the thorax and compress the developing lung. The diaphragm has four major embryologic contributions: septum transversum to the central tendon, pleuroperitoneal membranes to dorsolateral portions, dorsal mesentery of the esophagus to the crura, and body-wall mesoderm to peripheral muscular parts. The tested defect is therefore the pleuroperitoneal folds/membranes.
emphasis: failure of a pleuroperitoneal membrane to fuse

rationales.a: The dorsal mesentery of the esophagus forms the diaphragmatic crura; its abnormality is not the usual cause of a posterolateral Bochdalek hernia.
rationales.b: Pleuropericardial folds separate the pleural and pericardial cavities and contribute to fibrous pericardium, not the posterolateral diaphragm.
rationales.c: Body-wall mesoderm contributes peripheral diaphragmatic muscle, but the common congenital posterolateral hernia is due to failed pleuroperitoneal membrane closure.
